primary_meaning: Jesus Christ (as Savior/Son of God, via the ΙΧΘΥΣ/Ichthys acrostic)
primary_basis: Early Christian use of the Greek acrostic ΙΧΘΥΣ (Iēsous Christos Theou Yios Sōtēr) drawn from New Testament confessions of Jesus' identity (e.g., Matt 16:16; John 20:31; Rom 1:3-4)
Matt 4:19 / Mark 1:17 (call of the disciples as fishers of men, linking fish imagery to Christ and his mission)
John 21:1-14 (post-resurrection miraculous catch of fish associated with the risen Christ)
Matt 14:13-21 / Mark 6:30-44 / Luke 9:10-17 / John 6:1-14 (feeding miracles involving fish)

alternatives.meaning: Believers / Christians / the Church (as the 'catch' of the gospel)
basis: Matt 4:19 / Mark 1:17 / Luke 5:1-11 (fishers of men; disciples as fishers, people as fish)
John 21:1-14 (large catch of fish as image of mission and the gathered community)

alternatives.meaning: Divine provision, abundance, or eucharistic nourishment
basis: Matt 14:13-21 and parallels (multiplication of loaves and fish)
John 6 (Bread of Life discourse following the feeding; fish as part of the meal imagery)

alternatives.meaning: Typological sign of Christ's death, burial, and resurrection (via Jonah)
basis: Matt 12:39-41 / Matt 16:4 / Luke 11:29-32 (Jesus cites the sign of Jonah)

alternatives.meaning: Baptism / conversion / new life in the waters
basis: Association of fish with water and the fishers-of-men motif (Matt 4:19 etc.)
Early Christian artistic and catechetical links between fish imagery and baptismal rebirth

notes: The dominant, widely recognized Christian symbol of the fish is Christ himself via the Ichthys acrostic and early catacomb/art usage; related but secondary meanings (believers, provision, Jonah typology) are also standard in biblical interpretation and preaching. No major competing primary meaning displaces the Christ/Ichthys reading in mainstream Christian teaching.
